d: Explains Roblox support for mobile devices.
h:
The majority of Roblox sessions are played on mobile devices, so it's important to consider the mobile device orientation and other cross‑platform factors when designing a game for a wide audience.

To simplify cross‑platform inputs, including player interaction with virtual buttons, Roblox provides the Input Action System to define actions such as "jump," "sprint," or "shoot" and set up bindings for multiple hardware inputs to drive those actions.

Roblox also supports native mobile features like haptic feedback, touch gestures such as TouchSwipe and TouchPinch, or accelerometer and gyroscope functionality on AccelerometerEnabled and GyroscopeEnabled devices.

Input type detection

In cross‑platform development, it's important that you determine and respond to the PreferredInput type a player is using, normally to ensure that UI elements like on-screen buttons and menus work elegantly and support interaction across devices.

For example, a touch-enabled device assumes touch is the default input and that touch-buttons may appear for actions, but a player may choose to connect a bluetooth gamepad. In this case, touch remains a valid input, but you can assume the player wants to switch to the connected gamepad as the primary input type and possibly use touch as a backup input for on-screen UI.

See input type detection for more information.

Device orientation

By default, Roblox games run in landscape mode, allowing the game to switch between landscape "left" and landscape "right" as the player's device rotates. However, games can be locked to a particular orientation if desired.

There are five different orientation modes, including two sensor-based modes and three locked modes.¹ Each of these can be set as the default orientation through StarterGui.ScreenOrientation, accessible through Studio's Properties window.

Sensor Modes
LandscapeSensor The default Roblox setting in which the game always appears in landscape mode (no portrait mode) and the device detects its physical orientation to ensure the game view is always oriented upward.
Sensor The device detects its physical orientation to ensure the game view is always oriented upward, switching between landscape and portrait mode as needed.
Locked Modes
LandscapeLeft On devices with a virtual home/nav bar, its touch region is at the bottom of the display. On devices with a physical home button, the home button is to the left of the display.
LandscapeRight On devices with a virtual home/nav bar, its touch region is at the bottom of the display. On devices with a physical home button, the home button is to the right of the display.
Portrait On devices with a virtual home/nav bar, its touch region is at the bottom of the display. On devices with a physical home button, the home button is below the display.

Beyond the default StarterGui.ScreenOrientation property, you can change orientation during gameplay through PlayerGui.ScreenOrientation. This can be useful when a game needs to enforce an orientation, such as locking the view to Portrait for a minigame.

The following code in a LocalScript sets the screen orientation to portrait after a short delay:

LocalScript - Change Screen Orientation to Portrait

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local player = Players.LocalPlayer
local playerGui = player.PlayerGui

task.wait(5)

playerGui.ScreenOrientation = Enum.ScreenOrientation.Portrait

Finally, you can detect changes to screen orientation during gameplay by listening to value changes on the PlayerGui.CurrentScreenOrientation property.

LocalScript - Detect Screen Orientation Changes

local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local player = Players.LocalPlayer
local playerGui = player.PlayerGui

local function onOrientationChange()
    print("Orientation changed to", playerGui.ScreenOrientation)
end

playerGui:GetPropertyChangedSignal("ScreenOrientation"):Connect(onOrientationChange)

Haptic feedback

Most mobile devices have motors built in to provide haptic feedback. Adding rumbles and vibrations can greatly enhance a player's experience and provide subtle feedback beyond visuals or audio.

Roblox supports haptics for haptic-capable devices including most iPhone, Pixel, and Samsung Galaxy devices. Haptic feedback is managed through HapticEffect instances which can be set to a specific Type such as GameplayCollision or UIClick.

Once a HapticEffect is in place, you can initiate it through the Play() method, for instance:

local Workspace = game:GetService("Workspace")

local effect = Instance.new("HapticEffect")
effect.Type = Enum.HapticEffectType.GameplayExplosion
effect.Parent = Workspace

-- Play the haptic effect
effect:Play()

kid.simple: Most Roblox players play on phones and tablets, so your game needs to work well with touch. This page covers how to check what input a player is using, how to control whether the screen is sideways (landscape) or tall (portrait), and how to make the phone buzz with haptic feedback. Getting these right makes your game feel good in a player's hands.
kid.analogy: Screen orientation is like choosing to hold a book open sideways or upright. Haptic feedback is like a friend tapping your shoulder when something happens.
keyPoints: More Roblox sessions happen on mobile than anywhere else, so design for touch from the start.
Use the Input Action System for actions with on-screen buttons, and `PreferredInput` to see if a player switched to a gamepad or keyboard.
Mobile devices also support swipe and pinch gestures, plus accelerometer and gyroscope on devices that have them.
Games are landscape by default, using `LandscapeSensor`, which flips left or right as the phone turns.
Set the default orientation in `StarterGui.ScreenOrientation`: `LandscapeSensor`, `Sensor`, `LandscapeLeft`, `LandscapeRight`, or `Portrait`.
Change orientation during play with `PlayerGui.ScreenOrientation`, like locking to `Portrait` for a minigame.
Read `PlayerGui.CurrentScreenOrientation` to see which way the screen is actually showing.
Make the device vibrate with a `HapticEffect`, set its `Type`, and call `Play()`.

terms.orientation: Which way the screen is turned: sideways (landscape) or tall (portrait).
terms.landscape: The screen is wider than it is tall, like a TV.
terms.portrait: The screen is taller than it is wide, like a phone held normally.
terms.sensor mode: The phone uses its motion sensor to keep the game right-side up as you turn it.
terms.locked mode: The game stays in one orientation no matter how the phone is turned.
terms.haptic feedback: A small buzz or vibration from the device's motor that you can feel.
terms.accelerometer: A sensor that measures how the device is moving or tilting.
terms.gyroscope: A sensor that measures how the device is rotating.
terms.gesture: A touch movement like a swipe (sliding a finger) or a pinch (two fingers moving together or apart).

example.title: Lock to portrait and buzz the phone
example.code:
local Players = game:GetService("Players")

local player = Players.LocalPlayer
local playerGui = player:WaitForChild("PlayerGui")

-- Print whenever the real screen orientation changes
playerGui:GetPropertyChangedSignal("CurrentScreenOrientation"):Connect(function()
	print("Screen is now", playerGui.CurrentScreenOrientation)
end)

-- After 5 seconds, switch to portrait for a minigame
task.wait(5)
playerGui.ScreenOrientation = Enum.ScreenOrientation.Portrait

-- Give a little buzz to show something happened
local effect = Instance.new("HapticEffect")
effect.Type = Enum.HapticEffectType.UINotification
effect.Parent = workspace
effect:Play()
explain: We get the player's `PlayerGui`, which controls their screen.
We listen to `CurrentScreenOrientation` so we know whenever the screen actually turns.
After 5 seconds, we ask for `Portrait`, so the game shows tall like a normal phone.
We make a `HapticEffect` with the `UINotification` type and play it, so phones that support haptics give a short buzz.

watchOut: Forcing portrait mode for your whole game when most of it is designed for landscape. Lock it only when it makes sense.
Expecting every device to vibrate. Haptics only work on devices that support them.
Placing buttons where thumbs cannot reach or where the home bar sits. Test on a real phone or Studio's device emulator.
